messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan is a twenty-one-year-old married man who works as a social ministry worker in a mid-sized American city. Two years ago, he deployed overseas as a civilian relief worker during a period of active armed conflict. He was stationed near a forward operating base, and his role involved distributing food and medical supplies to displaced families in a region where Arabic was the dominant language. One afternoon, while his convoy was stopped at a checkpoint, a group of local men began shouting in Arabic. Ethan had heard shouting like that many times before, but this time the tone was different—urgent, angry, escalating. Before he could understand what was happening, gunfire erupted from a nearby building. He dove to the floor of the armored vehicle, and for what felt like an eternity he lay there, pressed against the metal, listening to the shouts and the shots and the screams of a colleague who had been hit. The colleague survived, but Ethan has never forgotten the sound of that voice, or the way his own body went cold with a terror so complete it felt like the world had stopped.

In the months that followed, Ethan returned home and tried to resume his life. But the memory of that afternoon does not behave like a normal memory. When he talks about the event—when a caseworker at his ministry asks him about his deployment, or when a veteran in his congregation mentions a combat experience—Ethan feels the same raw terror he felt on the floor of that vehicle. The memory does not feel like something that happened to him; it feels like something that is happening to him right now, in the present moment. Sometimes, when he tries to describe it to his wife, he stops mid-sentence because the story sounds so extreme, so far outside the realm of ordinary life, that he cannot believe it actually happened to him. He has come to wonder if he is losing his grip on reality.

Ethan’s work as a social ministry worker now places him in constant contact with the very things that terrify him. His office is in a neighborhood where many refugees and immigrants live, and he frequently hears Arabic spoken on the street. Every time he hears that language shouted—even in laughter, even in greeting—his body locks up and he scans for an exit. He has begun to avoid the parts of his route that pass by the local mosque, not because he holds any prejudice, but because the sound of Arabic voices in prayer or conversation sends him into a state of hypervigilance that lasts for hours. He is certain that strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations like a grocery store or a gas station, pose a threat. He watches their hands, their faces, their sudden movements. He has become so sensitive to motion that when someone turns quickly or raises an arm, he flinches and feels his heart hammer.

To manage this constant sense of danger, Ethan has developed a rigid set of nightly routines. He stays awake until two or three in the morning, delaying sleep because he knows that when he does finally close his eyes, he will wake repeatedly to check that he is safe. He listens for footsteps outside the bedroom door, for the creak of the stairs, for any sound that might signal an intrusion. His wife has grown frustrated with his refusal to go to bed at a normal hour, and she has started sleeping in the guest room. Ethan knows this is hurting their marriage, but he cannot bring himself to change the habit—it feels like the only thing keeping them safe.

He has also noticed that he avoids anything that might make him feel happy or hopeful. He turns down invitations to parties, to game nights with friends, to casual dinners. He has come to believe that if he lets himself feel good, something terrible will happen to punish him for it. Instead, he spends his evenings alone, replaying the event in his mind, trying to figure out how it could have been prevented. He runs through every detail: if he had noticed the men earlier, if he had told the driver to take a different route, if he had shouted back. The rumination gives him the illusion of control, but it also keeps the memory fresh and raw.

What finally brought Ethan to seek help was a moment last week when his wife told him she could not live like this anymore. She said she felt like she was married to a ghost. Ethan agreed to come to therapy, but he is terrified of what he might find. He is afraid that if he talks about the event in detail, he will be swallowed by the terror all over again. He is also afraid that he is broken in a way that cannot be fixed. What he hopes for, more than anything, is to feel like the memory belongs to the past—to be able to hear a voice raised in another language and not feel like he is back on that floor.
